scenes.heading: Indexing Strategies
scenes.narration: Indexes are auxiliary data structures that let a query engine find matching rows without scanning the entire table, trading extra storage and write cost for read speed.

scenes.heading: Common index types
bullets: B-tree for equality and range lookups
Zone maps and min-max skipping in lakehouses
scenes.narration: B-tree indexes are the workhorse for both equality and range queries and keep keys sorted for efficient traversal. Hash indexes give the fastest exact-match point lookups but cannot serve ranges. Bitmap indexes excel at low-cardinality columns in analytical workloads, letting the engine combine filters with bitwise operations. In lakehouses, lightweight zone maps and min-max statistics let the engine skip whole files whose ranges cannot match, which is index-like data skipping without a full index.

scenes.heading: Indexing tradeoffs
scenes.narration: Adding indexes speeds targeted reads and lets the engine answer queries without scanning the whole table, which is ideal for read-heavy tables and selective filters. But each index must be maintained on every write, so more indexes slow inserts and updates and consume extra storage, making a lean set better for write-heavy tables. The craft is indexing the columns that appear in selective WHERE and JOIN clauses while resisting the temptation to index everything.

scenes.heading: How an index speeds a lookup
steps: Query filters on an indexed column
Return results without a full scan
scenes.narration: When a query filters on an indexed column, the engine consults the index rather than the table. The index, being sorted or hashed, narrows down to the matching entries far faster than a scan. It returns the physical locations of the qualifying rows. The engine then fetches just those rows from storage. The result is returned without ever reading the vast majority of the table, which is the whole point of an index.

scenes.heading: Indexing in the lakehouse world
bullets: Data skipping via min-max file statistics
Clustering sorts data for effective skipping
Full secondary indexes are rare on the lake
scenes.narration: Indexing looks different on a data lake than in a traditional database. Instead of heavy secondary indexes, lakehouses lean on data skipping, using per-file min and max statistics to avoid reading files that cannot match a filter. Bloom filters cheaply test whether a value might exist in a file, letting the engine skip files that definitely do not contain it. Clustering the data by common filter columns makes that skipping far more effective. Full row-level secondary indexes are comparatively rare, because on large scans, skipping whole files is what matters most.

scenes.text: Index the selective columns your queries actually filter and join on, and let write cost stop you from over-indexing.
scenes.narration: Index the selective columns your queries genuinely filter and join on, and let the maintenance cost on every write be the discipline that stops you from over-indexing a table.
